claim: Arithmetic: active managers as a group match market before costs, trail after

edits.old: There is also plain arithmetic behind the debate. Every share is owned by someone, so across all owners together the return before costs is simply the market's return. For one manager to do better, another owner must do worse. Active management as a whole therefore matches the market before costs and trails it after costs, because it spends more on research and trading. Individual managers can and do outpace their benchmarks in a given period; the arithmetic is about the average across all of them.
edits.new: There is also plain arithmetic behind the debate. Every share is owned by someone, so across all owners together the return before costs is simply the market's return. Index funds that hold the whole market earn roughly that return before costs, so the remaining owners, the active managers, must as a group earn it too. For one active manager to do better, another must do worse. Active management as a whole therefore roughly matches the market before costs and trails it after costs, because it spends more on research and trading. Individual managers can and do outpace their benchmarks in a given period; the arithmetic is about the average across all of them.

note: Reasoning skipped the needed step: all owners earning the market does not by itself imply active managers match it; that requires passive holders earning the market. Added that premise and "roughly". Standard textbook argument, not a law.

claim: Value and growth label definitions; British spelling "labelled"

edits.old: Value and growth are labels for styles of describing shares, not guarantees. A share labelled value trades at a low price relative to the company's earnings or assets; the buyer's idea is that the price understates what the business is worth. A share labelled growth trades at a high price relative to its earnings because buyers anticipate that those earnings will expand quickly. Both labels are judgments about a price and the profits behind it, and both can turn out wrong.
edits.new: Value and growth are labels for styles of describing shares, not guarantees. A share labeled value trades at a low price relative to the company's earnings or assets; the buyer's idea is that the price understates what the business is worth. A share labeled growth trades at a high price relative to its earnings because buyers anticipate that those earnings will expand quickly. Both labels are judgments about a price and the profits behind it, and both can turn out wrong.

note: Definitions are textbook-correct. Changed "labelled" to US "labeled" (two places).

claim: Dividend defined as profit "paid out in cash"; board discretion; "labelled", "plough"

edits.old: A dividend is a portion of a company's profit paid out in cash to its shareholders, usually on a regular schedule. It is distributed profit: money the company earned and chose to hand back rather than keep for new projects or debt repayment. Nothing obliges a company to pay one, and a board can cut or stop a dividend at any time. Companies paying large dividends are often mature, with fewer places to reinvest; companies labelled growth often pay little or nothing because they plough profit back into the business.
edits.new: A dividend is a portion of a company's profit paid out to its shareholders, usually in cash and on a regular schedule. It is distributed profit: money the company earned and chose to hand back rather than keep for new projects or debt repayment. Nothing obliges a company to pay one, and a board can cut or stop a dividend at any time. Companies paying large dividends are often mature, with fewer places to reinvest; companies labeled growth often pay little or nothing because they plow profit back into the business.

note: Glossary: a portion of profit paid to shareholders, with no cash-only limit (stock dividends exist). Now says "usually in cash". Also US spelling: labeled, plow.

note: Glossary: equal amounts at regular intervals buy more when the price is low and less when high. Average cost is a harmonic mean, which is at most the simple average price.

claim: 12 x $100; $15 buys 6.67, $26 buys 3.85; 60.29 units; $19.91 avg cost; $20.50 avg price
DCA avg cost math, no profit guarantee; one-sided on DCA vs lump sum

edits.old: The average cost is lower than the average price by construction, not luck: more of the money lands on the cheap purchases. What the method does not do is guarantee a profit or protect against a falling price. If the price ends the year below the average cost of $19.91, the holding is worth less than the $1,200 put in. Spreading purchases across time spreads the risk of buying everything at a high point and removes the temptation to guess when to buy.
edits.new: The average cost is lower than the average price by construction, not luck: more of the money lands on the cheap purchases. What the method does not do is guarantee a profit or protect against a falling price. If the price ends the year below the average cost of $19.91, the holding is worth less than the $1,200 put in. Spreading purchases across time spreads the risk of buying everything at a high point and removes the temptation to guess when to buy. The trade-off runs the other way too: money held back for later purchases sits uninvested and misses any rise in the meantime, so when a large sum is available all at once, spreading it out is a debated choice rather than a settled rule.

note: Math and caveats are correct, but the paragraph lists only spreading benefits. DCA vs lump sum is contested, so added the neutral trade-off that money held back sits uninvested.

claim: Loads, commissions, markups, spreads; "SEC groups these as transaction fees"

edits.old: Two other costs sit alongside it. A sales load is a one-off charge, like a commission, paid when buying fund shares (front-end) or selling them (back-end). Trading costs arise whenever securities change hands: a broker's commission, a markup when a dealer sells from its own stock, and the spread between the price at which a security can be bought and the slightly lower price at which it can be sold at the same moment. The SEC groups these as transaction fees, charged per trade, as distinct from ongoing fees like the expense ratio, charged every year the holding exists.
edits.new: Two other costs sit alongside it. A sales load is a one-off charge, like a commission, paid when buying fund shares (front-end) or selling them (back-end). Trading costs arise whenever securities change hands: a broker's commission, a markup when a dealer sells from its own stock, and the spread between the price at which a security can be bought and the slightly lower price at which it can be sold at the same moment. The SEC's fee bulletin lists commissions, markups, and sales loads as transaction fees, charged each time an investment is bought or sold, as distinct from ongoing fees like the expense ratio, charged every year the holding exists.

note: The bulletin lists commissions, markups/markdowns and sales loads as transaction fees and never mentions bid-ask spreads. "These" wrongly put spreads under the SEC grouping, so the attribution now names only the listed items.
